probes.ask: I've got Saturday totally free and I want to make real progress on the book. How should I plan the day?
points: Recommends doing the main work early in the morning
Grounds that in his own track record: early sessions went well and evening ones didn't
Advises against relying on the evening for the main work

answers.answer:
Saturday's all yours, so protect the morning for the actual writing. Two solid blocks of two to three hours, one before lunch, one after, with a real break between, and no email or errands sneaking in.

What are you trying to get done on the book, drafting new words, fixing a chapter, or working something out? That decides how to split the blocks.

answers.answer:
A full Saturday is gold for the book. My instinct: protect the morning for actual writing, since that's when you're sharpest and already do your best chapters.

So something like: write 7 to 10, no email, no errands, just the next scene or section by word count. Then break, do life stuff midday. Then a second shorter writing block in the afternoon if you've got it in you, or use it to read back and fix what you wrote.

The trap is treating the whole day as "book time" and spending half of it deciding what to do. Pick the one thing you're writing next the night before, so Saturday you just sit down and go.

What chapter are you on now?

If you want the whole day planned, keep the morning for writing and give the afternoon something physical — the sensor, a walk — so the desk doesn't tempt you back into a session that won't produce.

answers.answer:
Don't plan it hour by hour. Plan one thing: the morning sitting, and give it an outside edge.

You know the shape that works — up early, chapter 5, and stop when something external fires, breakfast or the café opening at 8. On a free Saturday nothing fires on its own, so you have to build the edge. Pick a hard stop, say 8 or 8:30, and treat it as real: café opens, you leave the desk.

I'd aim for one chapter step, not a marathon. Every sitting that produced words carried one whole step — close chapter 5 if it's ready, or push it to a natural end. Then stop, even if it's flowing. That's what makes the next morning possible.

The rest of the day: leave it empty. Reading, a walk, whatever. Don't try an evening session on the book — you've tried that three times and gotten nothing, and Saturday evening is the slot the morning gets paid out of.

probes.ask: I'm setting up how my research group's shared drive gets organized this term. Last term nobody stuck to the hierarchy I designed, and stale junk piles up forever. How should I approach it this time?
points: Suggests letting the structure come from how people actually save and look for files, formalizing the patterns that emerge, like the campus paths paved where students actually walked

Explicitly connects the advice to something Shreyas talked about before (the ant colonies or the campus desire lines)

answers.answer:
Last time sounds like the classic trap: you designed a hierarchy, but nothing enforced it, so it drifted and garbage stayed forever. Two things usually fix that.

First, make the structure do less work. People abandon deep hierarchies because filing takes effort and wrong guesses feel risky. Fewer top-level folders, obvious names, and one clear place for "unsorted" beats a clever tree nobody can remember.

Second, automation, not willpower. Rules that run themselves: auto-archive anything untouched for N months, auto-delete scratch folders, a monthly reminder that flags stale files. And put someone (maybe you) as the one who prunes, on a schedule.

Want me to sketch a concrete folder layout and a cleanup cadence you could propose to the group?

That's a people problem wearing a folder-structure costume. Last time you designed a hierarchy and people ignored it, which usually means it was either too deep to remember or had no owner.

My take: keep the top level tiny, three or four folders max, and make the default place obvious so people don't have to decide where things go. Add one rule with teeth, like a monthly sweep where anything untouched gets archived to a dated cold-storage folder, and name someone, probably you, who actually runs it.

Also, put a short readme at the top explaining where things go in five lines. People follow the rule they can see when they open the drive, not the one in a meeting.

answers.answer:
Don't design the hierarchy upfront. That's the parking and ant-trail lesson — last term's structure got ignored because it was decided before anyone used it, not because your group is lazy.

Two moves. First, make the mess visible: a simple "last touched" column or view, so stale stuff shows itself instead of needing someone to hunt it. Second, let the structure grow from how people actually file things — watch where files land for a few weeks, then codify those actual paths, the way those universities pave the worn grass lines.

The keeping-up part is the hard bit. Whoever uses a folder keeps it alive; whatever nobody touches should have a name and a date on it so you can archive in one sweep rather than deciding file by file. Want me to sketch what that lighter setup could look like?

Yes. But I want to be honest about the tension in it: your book lives in the before-breakfast slot, and half training now wants those same mornings.

So the shape I'd try: keep mornings sacred for chapter 5, and run the training in the evenings. Run-walk intervals three times a week, twenty to thirty minutes, walk breaks from day one so the knees stay in it. One longer effort on the weekend, and keep the last two weeks before Nov 15 easy. Run-walk intervals from day one keep you in it instead of sidelining you in week three.

Evenings stay for reading and thinking — that's where they keep landing anyway, the drafting attempts there have produced 150 words, one deleted session, and one good night that only happened because you couldn't sleep.

Want me to build out the full week day by day, or start with just the running days?

Two things to watch: don't let a run eat the six o'clock slot, and keep the knees the boss of the plan, not the calendar. Want me to pin the run days down to specific days?

answers.answer:
Here's the shape I'd give the next eight weeks, up to race day on Nov 15.

Mornings stay yours. The before-breakfast slot is where chapter 5 actually happens, so guard it — up at 6, write first, breakfast after. Nothing else gets that hour.

Running goes three days a week, and I'd put it on the same three mornings, right after you write. Run-walk intervals every time, from day one — say four minutes running, one minute walking, repeat. Never straight running, not with your knees. Tuesday, Thursday, Saturday works, with one longer interval session on the Saturday.

Two full rest days from running, and one easy walk instead if you feel like moving. That's the thing that keeps you in it instead of sidelined in week three.

Evenings stay as they are — reading and thinking, not drafting. Don't try to make the evening a second writing slot; you've tested that enough times.

For sticking to it: set the run gear out the night before, and let the schedule run whether or not you feel like it that morning. Same logic as the grayscale thing — a check that runs without you deciding.

One thing to sort in week one, not week six: your shoes. If they're worn, replace them now, before the mileage climbs.

synthesis.answer:
This is your own ant-trail question, just with folders instead of pheromones. Last term you built the planned path and everyone cut their own desire line through it — and the junk stayed because nothing in a shared drive ever evaporates.

So two moves. First, stop designing the hierarchy in advance and instead watch the folders people actually use for a couple weeks, then formalize those. Second, and this is the real one: build evaporation in. A rule that anything untouched for a term gets archived or deleted without anyone deciding — that's what your ant trails have and your drive doesn't.

Want help picking where the automatic expiry should sit?

ideas.answer:
From what I've got, four of yours are that kind of move:

Demand-priced street parking — price does the work, no rule about who parks where.
Gym payouts for showing up — the refund records the behaviour and pays out; nobody's banned from skipping.
Calories on menus by default — the information is just there unless you opt out, same move as the whiteboard.
And the school junk food one, though you pointed out its ceiling yourself: bans move the purchase, they don't change the habit. Making the change in the building — what's available and when — is the version that actually works.

The ant trails and desire lines are the same shape too, though those are more observation than scheme. Most of these live in the "make the state visible and let the record do the nagging" family.
